rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts say Moses retreated when the staff became a serpent, without returning; the commentary points to these parallels.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere in the Quran, when the staff becomes a serpent, Moses is said to have turned in retreat without returning

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Moses' fear subsided when God promised to restore the serpent to its former form, meaning the staff.
rows.anchor: Some say that Moses’fear was assuaged when God informed him that He would cause the serpent to return to its former way

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Others say that after God said not to fear, tranquility and contentment came over Moses and ended his fear.
rows.anchor: Yet others say that after God told Moses not to fear, a state of tranquility and contentment overcame him so that he was no longer fearful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses seized the serpent by its mouth, either at the teeth or jaw, and God turned it back into a wooden staff.
rows.anchor: Moses then laid hold of the serpent by its mouth, grabbing it by either the teeth or the jaw

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says God showed Moses the serpent beforehand so he would not fear when he later cast the staff before Pharaoh and his entourage.
rows.anchor: Al-Qurṭubīexplains that God showed Moses the serpent as a way of preparing him

rows.speaker: philosophers and mystics
rows.claim: They read the staff-serpent as the unrefined lower soul, which must be conquered for the soul's true nature to be realized.
rows.anchor: Some philosophers and mystics read this verse as alluding to various aspects of the human being’s lower nature

rows.speaker: Mullā Ṣadrā
rows.claim: Mullā Ṣadrā urges purifying and subduing the soul until it returns to its primordial disposition and lives intellectually, striving for the Return and Final Abode.
rows.anchor: as explained by Mullā Ṣadrā: “There is no serpent like your soul; so slay it and purify it of the stain of its false beliefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims commonly recite this prayer in times of difficulty and anxiety.
rows.anchor: This part of Moses’ prayer is commonly uttered by Muslims at times of difficulty and anxiety

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation of the expanded breast is a prayer for God to fill Moses with the light of faith and certainty.
rows.anchor: Moses’ prayer for his breast to be expanded is seen as a prayer to God to fill his being with the light of faith and certainty

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that the expanded breast would help Moses carry out his message properly.
rows.anchor: or to help him carry out his message properly

rows.speaker: some Muslim and Jewish commentators
rows.claim: Some Muslim and Jewish commentators take the knot as a physical speech impediment, namely a lisp.
rows.anchor: some Muslim and Jewish commentators (see 26:12–13c) to be a reference to a physical speech impediment

rows.speaker: the commentators
rows.claim: Commentators relate that, as a child, Moses struck Pharaoh and pulled hair from his beard, which Pharaoh took as a sign Moses would become his enemy and destroy his kingdom.
rows.anchor: The commentators relate a story that, while still a child, Moses struck Pharaoh and pulled some of the hair out of his beard

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Pharaoh already feared an Israelite son would overthrow him, perhaps explaining his order to kill the Israelite boys.
rows.anchor: according to some, Pharaoh had already developed a fear that one of the sons of the Israelites would overthrow him

rows.speaker: the commentators
rows.claim: Āsiyah defended Moses as too young to distinguish right from wrong; Pharaoh tested him with a ruby and fiery coal, threatening death if he chose the ruby and acquitting him if he chose coal.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh’s wife Āsiyah (regarding whom see 66:11c) tried to protect Moses, assuring him that Moses was just a young child

rows.speaker: the commentators
rows.claim: Gabriel guided Moses to the coal; Moses put it in his mouth, burned his tongue, and thereby acquired the speech impediment.
rows.anchor: Gabriel came and guided his hand to lay hold of the fiery coal, which Moses then accidentally placed into his mouth

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says Moses sought to loosen the knot so he could effectively deliver God's commission, as the following phrase clarifies.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī observes that Moses’ request that God untie a knot from his tongue was motivated by his desire to be able to communicate effectively

rows.speaker: Ibn Juzayy
rows.claim: Ibn Juzayy says Moses asked only for partial relief, enough for people to understand clearly, rather than complete eloquence.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn Juzayy, the reason Moses requested that God only loosen and not completely remove a knot from his tongue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' request was granted, as the commentary points to the later verse.
rows.anchor: Moses’request was granted, for which, see v. 36c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary suggests Moses linked an expanded breast and loosened tongue because rejection and accusations of lying would constrict him and impede his speech.
rows.anchor: It is also possible that there is a connection between Moses’ request that his breast be expanded and that a knot in his tongue be loosened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's signs here are the nine signs given to Moses.
rows.anchor: My signs refers to the nine signs given to Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not tiring in God's remembrance means not weakening in conveying the message.
rows.anchor: Tire not in the remembrance of Me means to not weaken in conveying the message

rows.speaker: spiritual interpretation
rows.claim: A spiritual reading warns against invoking God with the tongue while the heart remains inattentive to the One invoked.
rows.anchor: According to a spiritual interpretation of this verse, it means that one should not invoke God only with the tongue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers either to the earth or to dust, which can also mean earth.
rows.anchor: It here refers to the earth (arḍ; Ṭ) or dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is often recited at Muslim funerals to recall that people are made from earth or clay, buried in it, and resurrected from it.
rows.anchor: This verse is often recited at Muslim funerals, as it instructs people that human beings are made of earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, Moses warns them not to label God's signs and miracles sorcery.
rows.anchor: In this context, Moses’ words Do not fabricate a lie against God mean,“Do not call God’s signs and miracles sorcery”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses spoke, the sorcerers privately consulted on the best way to oppose and overcome him.
rows.anchor: Upon hearing Moses’ words, the sorcerers consulted one another in private concerning the best means by which they could oppose and overcome him

rows.speaker: al-Māturīdī
rows.claim: Al-Māturīdī notes that the sorcerers' claim that Moses and Aaron sought to expel them echoes Pharaoh's identical earlier claim.
rows.anchor: Al-Māturīdī, the important Quran commentator and founder of the Māturīdī school of Sunni theology, notes that the sorcerers’ statement that Moses and Aaron wish to expel them from their land is taken from an identical statement by Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their accusation of sorcery refers to Moses' earlier miracles before Pharaoh, the nine signs that Pharaoh treated as sorcery.
rows.anchor: Their sorcery refers to the miracles that Moses performed for Pharaoh earlier

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sorcerers meant their comfortable lifestyle, with the Israelites meeting their needs because Egypt dominated them.
rows.anchor: By their exemplary way of life the sorcerers were referring to their easy lifestyle, which entailed all of their needs being met by the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses feared the spectacle might keep the people from recognizing the truth of his sign after the sorcerers made their ropes appear as serpents.
rows.anchor: Moses conceived a fear in his soul means fear entered into his heart because, after the sorcerers had caused their ropes to appear as serpents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's inhabitants neither die nor live because they have no rest and no life from which they can draw positive benefit.
rows.anchor: One neither dies nor lives in Hell because its inhabitants will not experience rest in it, nor will they live a kind of life from which they can draw positive benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers readers to its discussion of the various ranks in Paradise.
rows.anchor: For the various ranks in Paradise, see 4:96c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran mentions the Gardens of Eden in several other places.
rows.anchor: The Gardens of Eden are mentioned in several places in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that the Prophet feared forgetting revelation and quickly repeated Gabriel's words while they were being revealed.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the Prophet’s fear of forgetting the verses of revelation, which led him to repeat quickly what was being revealed to him by the Archangel Gabriel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the verse admonishes the Prophet not to seek revelation before its proper time.
rows.anchor: Alternatively, it could be an admonishment to the Prophet not to seek to receive the revelation before its appropriate time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims commonly use the plea for increased knowledge, including students beginning their studies.
rows.anchor: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge! is commonly invoked by Muslims at various times, such as when they are students beginning their studies

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to pray that God not bless a day on which he gains no knowledge that brings him nearer to God.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said, “If a day comes upon me in which I do not increase in a knowledge that draws me nearer to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Prophet is told to ask for more knowledge, all Muslims should do so a fortiori.
rows.anchor: Thus, if the Prophet is told to pray for increase in knowledge, then, a fortiori, all Muslims are expected to do the same

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī says the supplication is presented to the community so they too will seek increase from God; if exclusive to the Prophet, that would have been made clear.
rows.anchor: Hence, Ibn ʿArabī says, “God did not say to His Prophet, Say, ‘My Lord! Increase me in knowledge!’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufis particularly use this supplication, though pious Muslims generally use it as well.
rows.anchor: This supplication has often been a prayer of the Sufis in particular, although it is used by pious Muslims in general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's pact with Adam was the prohibition against approaching the tree.
rows.anchor: The pact that God made with Adam refers to His telling him not to approach the tree

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aforetime” can mean before Adam ate from the tree or, more broadly, before Muhammad's prophethood and Quranic revelation.
rows.anchor: By aforetime is meant either before Adam’s actual eating from the tree or, more generally, before the coming of the Prophet Muhammad and the revelation of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He forgot” can mean Adam forgot his pact or abandoned it.
rows.anchor: He forgot denotes Adam’s forgetting his pact (Q) or abandoning it

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that Adam forgot and so his descendants forgot.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said, “Adam forgot, and thus his progeny forgot.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam is a model for humanity; God taught him all the names.
rows.anchor: Adam is the model for human beings to follow, since God taught Adam the names, all of them

rows.speaker: Shams-i Tabrīzī
rows.claim: Shams says Adam forgot only once, so people should remember that one lapse is enough; his father's custom was to forget once.
rows.anchor: Shams-i Tabrīzī (disappeared in 644/1247), people should keep in mind that Adam only forgot one time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that Adam lacked resolve to disobey God, so his error was unintentional because Satan deceived him.
rows.anchor: We found no resoluteness in him can mean that God did not find in Adam the resolve to disobey Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that Adam lacked resolve to obey the prohibition; some connect this to his not being among the resolute messengers.
rows.anchor: Or We found no resoluteness in him can mean that God did not find in Adam the moral resolve to obey His Prohibition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary links God's warning to Adam and Eve that Satan is their enemy to another account.
rows.anchor: For the warning to Adam and Eve that Satan is an enemy unto them, see 7:21–22c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning means Adam and Eve must not obey Satan, who would deceive them into eating from the forbidden tree and drive them from the Garden.
rows.anchor: Let him not expel the two of you from the Garden is an admonition from God to Adam and Eve that they should not obey Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wretched” refers to the hardship and fatigue of earning a livelihood in the world after leaving the Garden's comfort.
rows.anchor: Such that thou wouldst be wretched refers to the hardship and fatigue that Adam and Eve would experience because of the need to earn a livelihood in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The absence of hunger, nakedness, thirst, and sun's heat evokes the Garden's ease, contrasted with worldly hardship after yielding to Satan.
rows.anchor: Thus, the references in v. 118 to being neither hungry nor naked, and in v. 119 to neither being thirsty nor experiencing the sun’s heat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary points to other accounts of the warning, Satan's deception, the fall, and Adam and Eve's remorse.
rows.anchor: For other accounts of Adam and Eve’s being warned by God, Satan’s deceiving them, their fall from Paradise, and their remorse over their actions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is understood to include Adam, Eve, and their future descendants, announcing their banishment from Paradise.
rows.anchor: This verse is understood to be an address to Adam and Eve and their future progeny, indicating their banishment from Paradise

words: فَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَ هُدَاىَ فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following God's guidance on earth is the means by which humanity can recover its original nature after the fall.
rows.anchor: but also the means by which they could recover their original nature while on earth—by following God’s Guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “My remembrance” can mean the Quran specifically, as “My Reminder,” or God's guidance generally, which reminds people of Him and calls them to Him.
rows.anchor: The remembrance of Me can refer to the Quran in particular

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A miserable life can mean a constricted life, especially spiritually.
rows.anchor: A miserable life is a life that is constricted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it is a worldly life focused on possessions and fear of losing them, contrasted with believers' hope in the Hereafter and life blessed by faith.
rows.anchor: Or, it may refer to a life in which one is merely given to the things of the world and lives in a state where he is fearful of their being taken away from him

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts this miserable life with the believer's good life described in 16:97.
rows.anchor: Juxtaposing such people with the believers, al-Zamakhsharī calls attention to 16:97

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afterlife blindness can occur despite earthly physical sight; it directly reflects spiritual blindness in this life.
rows.anchor: Some people are said to be raised blind on the Last Day and in the Hereafter, even though they could see with their physical sight while alive on earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, those spiritually blind in this life will see the realities they rejected with clarity in the next life.
rows.anchor: From another perspective, those who were spiritually blind in this life will come to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting God's signs means abandoning and disbelieving in them, namely the proofs brought by His messengers.
rows.anchor: To forget Our signs (v. 126) means to abandon and disbelieve in God’s signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers to other passages on God forgetting the disbelievers on the Last Day.
rows.anchor: For God’s “forgetting”the disbelievers on the Last Day, see 7:51c and 45:34c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the meaning of “the prodigal,” the commentary refers to 10:12.
rows.anchor: For the prodigal, see 10:12c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that perpetual afterlife blindness is more intense than any constriction experienced in worldly life.
rows.anchor: The promise that the chastisement of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting means that the disbeliever’s perpetual blindness in the Hereafter is more intense than any kind of constriction that he will experience in this life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, God's leaving the disbeliever blind in the Hereafter is more intense and lasts longer than the blindness caused by turning from God's signs.
rows.anchor: Alternately, it can mean that God’s leaving the disbeliever in his state of blindness in the Hereafter is more intense and longer-lasting than the blindness that results from his turning away from God’s signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Makkans repeatedly demanded that the Prophet bring a sign.
rows.anchor: The Makkans made repeated requests for the Prophet to bring them a sign

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear proof may refer to Quranic stories also found in earlier scriptures, which demonstrate the Quran's divine source.
rows.anchor: The clear proof of that which is in the scriptures of old is a reference to the various stories in the Quran that are also found in the previous scriptures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it may refer to Torah and Gospel passages that mention Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Alternatively, this part of the verse can be a reference to those parts of the Torah and the Gospel that mention the Prophet Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each party waits to see its outcome, either in this life or at death.
rows.anchor: That each is waiting means each party is waiting to see what its outcome will be, either in this life or at the time of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that they will come to know is meant to threaten and frighten the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: The words for you shall come to know are intended to threaten and frighten the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Preserved” can mean guarded from satans, or elevated and protected from falling upon the earth.
rows.anchor: Preserved means preserved from the satans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky as a canopy is also described elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: is also mentioned in 2:22; 40:64; 79:28

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters turn away from the heavens' signs, including the sun, moon, and stars.
rows.anchor: It is said the idolaters turn away in the face of the signs of the heavens, including the sun, moon, and stars
